title: Enums, Pattern Matching & Error Handling
scopeHtml: Scope: Enums with associated values, switch pattern matching, Result, throws/try/catch, typed throws, Never, optionals as enums.

notes.title: Baseline and the big picture
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you model "one of several shapes" with sealed class / sealed interface, model absence with T?, and model failure with exceptions or Result<T>. In Swift the same three jobs are done by one feature: the enum. Optional<T> is itself an enum, Result<Success, Failure> is an enum, and errors are values conforming to the Error protocol (usually enums).

Baseline for every note in this track: Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first. Modern APIs are shown first. Legacy forms (completion handlers, Result as the main async tool, NSError) are labelled "you will meet this in old codebases". Anything fast-moving is marked verify.

Kotlin world                    Swift world
-----------------------------   -----------------------------
sealed class / interface        enum with associated values
T? (nullable)                   Optional<T>  == enum { none, some(T) }
Result<T> / try-catch           throws + do/catch, Result<S, F>
Nothing                         Never (an enum with zero cases)
when (exhaustive)               switch (exhaustive, always)
Android (Kotlin) iOS (Swift)
sealed interface UiState enum UiState
data class Loaded(val items: List<Item>) case loaded(items: [Item])
when (state) { is Loaded -> ... } switch state { case .loaded(let items): ... }
throw IOException() throw MyError.io
runCatching { } Result { try ... }
Nothing Never

Everyday analogy, after the idea: an enum is a vending machine slot label. Each slot is exactly one product (a case), and some slots hold extra stuff (associated values). You cannot be in two slots at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Swift enums are like Java enums". They are far closer to Kotlin sealed classes plus ADTs (algebraic data types).
  • Forgetting that Optional is an enum; interviewers love "how is nil implemented?".
  • Assuming Swift uses checked exceptions; Swift errors are checked for propagation (you must write try) but not for type (until typed throws).

notes.title: Enums with associated values vs Kotlin sealed classes
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you model screen state as sealed interface UiState { object Loading; data class Success(val items: List<Item>); data class Error(val msg: String) }. In iOS you write one enum and put the payload directly on the case.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum LoadState {
    case idle
    case loading
    case loaded(items: [Item])
    case failed(message: String, retryable: Bool)
}

let state: LoadState = .failed(message: "Offline", retryable: true)
sealed interface LoadState {
    data object Idle : LoadState
    data object Loading : LoadState
    data class Loaded(val items: List<Item>) : LoadState
    data class Failed(val message: String, val retryable: Boolean) : LoadState
}

val state: LoadState = LoadState.Failed("Offline", true)

Key differences from Kotlin:

  • One declaration, no subclasses. Each case is not a type. In Kotlin Loaded is its own class you can pass around; in Swift .loaded is only a constructor of LoadState. You cannot write a function taking "only the loaded case".
  • Value semantics. An enum is a value type (stored inline, no heap allocation unless a payload needs it). Kotlin sealed subclasses are heap objects.
  • Memory layout. Swift stores the payload plus a small tag. MemoryLayout<LoadState>.size is the max payload size plus tag bits; the compiler reuses spare bits (extra inhabitants) in pointers so Optional<SomeClass> is the same size as a pointer (8 bytes), with nil being the all-zero bit pattern. That is why Optional of a reference type is free.
  • Raw values are a different feature: enum Status: Int { case ok = 200 } gives you rawValue and init?(rawValue:). An enum cannot have both raw values and associated values.
  • Methods, computed properties and protocol conformance go directly on the enum. There are no stored properties, only computed ones.
extension LoadState {
    var isLoading: Bool {
        if case .loading = self { return true }
        return false
    }
}

Automatic conformances: an enum with no associated values gets Equatable/Hashable for free; with payloads you write : Equatable and the compiler synthesises it if every payload is Equatable. CaseIterable gives allCases (only for payload-free enums). Codable is synthesised for both, with a documented JSON shape for associated values (a nested object keyed by case name, with _0, _1 keys for unlabelled payloads) since Swift 5.5 (SE-0295).

Real industry usage. The Swift Composable Architecture (Point-Free) models actions as one big enum, e.g. enum Action { case buttonTapped; case response(Result<Data, Error>) }; the whole app's events are an enum tree. Apple's own URLSession Task states, ScenePhase (.active, .inactive, .background), and SwiftUI AsyncImagePhase (.empty, .success(Image), .failure(Error)) are payload enums. Airbnb and Uber's Swift code bases use enums for screen state in the same way Android teams use sealed UiState.

Analogy: a sealed Kotlin class is a family tree of different shaped boxes; a Swift enum is a single box with a rotating label and a pocket that holds exactly what that label needs.

Common interview traps.

  • "Can a case be passed as a type?" No. Cases are not types in Swift (Kotlin subclasses are).
  • Forgetting that enum payload labels are optional but useful: case failed(String, Bool) compiles, but call sites become unreadable.
  • Putting stored properties on an enum (compile error). Use computed properties or an associated value.
  • Treating raw-value enums and associated-value enums as combinable; they are not.

notes.title: Exhaustive switch, where clauses and pattern matching
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin when on a sealed type is exhaustive only when used as an expression (or since Kotlin 1.7 as a statement for sealed/enum). Swift's switch is always exhaustive, as a statement and as an expression.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func title(for state: LoadState) -> String {
    switch state {
    case .idle: return "Ready"
    case .loading: return "Loading..."
    case .loaded(let items) where items.isEmpty: return "Nothing here"
    case .loaded(let items): return "\(items.count) items"
    case .failed(let message, _): return message
    }
}
fun title(state: LoadState): String = when (state) {
    LoadState.Idle -> "Ready"
    LoadState.Loading -> "Loading..."
    is LoadState.Loaded ->
        if (state.items.isEmpty()) "Nothing here" else "${state.items.size} items"
    is LoadState.Failed -> state.message
}

Since Swift 5.9 (SE-0380) if and switch can be expressions:

let label = switch state {
case .idle: "Ready"
case .loading: "Loading..."
case .loaded(let items): "\(items.count) items"
case .failed(let message, _): message
}

Pattern kinds you must know:

Pattern Example
Enum case + bind case .loaded(let items)
Bind everything case let .failed(msg, retry)
Ignore case .failed(_, true)
Value/literal case 200
Range case 200..<300
Tuple case (0, _)
Type test case let v as Int
Optional case .some(let x) or case let x?
Where case .loaded(let i) where i.count > 10
Multiple case .idle, .loading:

Other control flow forms that use the same patterns:

if case .loaded(let items) = state { print(items.count) }   // one-case test
guard case .loaded(let items) = state else { return }         // early exit
for case let .loaded(items) in states { }                     // filter loop
while case .some(let x) = iterator.next() { }
let isDone = if case .loaded = state { true } else { false }

No implicit fallthrough in Swift: each case body runs and exits. Use the fallthrough keyword if you really need it (rare). Every case needs at least one statement.

@unknown default. For enums from Apple frameworks that may gain cases in future iOS versions (non-frozen enums) the compiler warns if you do not handle new cases:

switch UNAuthorizationStatus {   // illustrative
case .authorized, .provisional, .ephemeral: break
case .denied, .notDetermined: break
@unknown default: break          // warning if a new case ships
}

Use @unknown default, not plain default, so the compiler tells you when a new OS adds a case. Plain default silently swallows new cases and is a classic source of "it broke on iOS 18" bugs.

Real industry usage. Reducers in TCA are a giant switch action. Apple's LocalAuthentication error codes and CLAuthorizationStatus are handled with @unknown default in sample code. Pattern matching on Result and Optional is how most older networking layers (Alamofire 4/5 response.result) were consumed.

Analogy: an exhaustive switch is an airport security gate with one lane for every passenger type. If a new passenger type is invented and no lane exists, the airport (the compiler) refuses to open.

Common interview traps.

  • Using default on your own enum: it hides missing cases when you add one later. Prefer listing all cases.
  • Expecting case .a, .b(let x) to bind: multiple patterns binding different variables must bind the same names and types.
  • Confusing if case .x = value (pattern) with if value == .x (needs Equatable).
  • Thinking a Swift switch falls through like C/Java.

notes.title: Indirect enums and recursive data
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin a recursive sealed hierarchy (sealed class Expr { class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) }) just works because objects live on the heap and are referenced. In Swift an enum is a value type; a case that contains its own type would have infinite size, so you opt into a heap box with indirect.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
indirect enum Expr {
    case number(Double)
    case add(Expr, Expr)
    case multiply(Expr, Expr)
    case negate(Expr)
}

func eval(_ e: Expr) -> Double {
    switch e {
    case .number(let n): return n
    case .add(let l, let r): return eval(l) + eval(r)
    case .multiply(let l, let r): return eval(l) * eval(r)
    case .negate(let x): return -eval(x)
    }
}

let tree: Expr = .add(.number(2), .multiply(.number(3), .number(4)))
sealed interface Expr {
    data class Number(val v: Double) : Expr
    data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr
    data class Multiply(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr
    data class Negate(val x: Expr) : Expr
}

fun eval(e: Expr): Double = when (e) {
    is Expr.Number -> e.v
    is Expr.Add -> eval(e.l) + eval(e.r)
    is Expr.Multiply -> eval(e.l) * eval(e.r)
    is Expr.Negate -> -eval(e.x)
}

Details:

  • indirect enum boxes all payload cases; indirect case add(Expr, Expr) boxes only that case. The box is a reference-counted heap allocation, so you pay ARC retain/release on copies of the node.
  • Copies are still logically value copies: the tree is immutable, so sharing the box is safe.
  • Recursion depth is limited by the stack. A tree 100,000 levels deep will overflow the stack when evaluated recursively (and even on deinit, because releasing a deep linked structure recurses). Real fix: iterate, or flatten to arrays with indices.
  • A struct cannot contain itself directly either; use a class, an array ([Node] is already a heap buffer) or indirect.

Real industry usage. Expression parsers, JSON value trees (enum JSON { case object([String: JSON]); case array([JSON]) ... } is allowed without indirect because Array/Dictionary already box), AST in SwiftSyntax and Point-Free's parser libraries, undo/redo command trees, and file-system trees.

Analogy: indirect is putting a Russian doll's inner doll in a separate box with a sticker address, instead of trying to fit an infinite stack of dolls inside each other.

Common interview traps.

  • "Why does this enum not compile?" (recursive value type with no indirection). The answer is indirect or a collection.
  • Assuming indirect is free; it adds heap allocation and ARC traffic.
  • Forgetting that deep recursion can crash on deinit as well as on eval.

notes.title: Optionals as enums
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin, String? is a compiler-level nullable reference with no wrapper object. In Swift, String? is literally Optional<String>, an enum, and you can pattern match on it.

// Conceptually how the standard library defines it
enum Optional<Wrapped> {
    case none
    case some(Wrapped)
}

let name: String? = "Ada"
switch name {
case .some(let n): print(n)
case .none: print("nobody")
}
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
let user: User? = repo.find(id)
if let user { print(user.name) }                    // if-let shorthand, Swift 5.7
guard let user else { return }                      // early exit
let n = user?.address?.city ?? "Unknown"            // chaining + default
let upper = user.map { $0.name.uppercased() }        // map over optional
let first = users.first { $0.age > 30 }             // returns User?
val user: User? = repo.find(id)
user?.let { println(it.name) }
val u = user ?: return
val n = user?.address?.city ?: "Unknown"
val upper = user?.let { it.name.uppercase() }
val first = users.firstOrNull { it.age > 30 }

Rules to remember:

  • ! force unwrap traps (crash) on nil: the crash text is Fatal error: Unexpectedly found nil while unwrapping an Optional value. It is the most common Swift crash in production crash reports.
  • T! (implicitly unwrapped optional) is an Optional that auto-unwraps; use it for @IBOutlet and two-phase init only.
  • Optional chaining returns an optional; a?.b?.c yields C?.
  • flatMap on Optional avoids T??. try? flattens since Swift 5 (no more double optionals).
  • Optional conforms to Equatable when Wrapped does; nil == nil is true.
  • Optional of an enum with spare bits can be packed with no extra storage; Int? needs 9 bytes (stride 16), a quirk interviewers like.

Android vs iOS: Kotlin has smart-casts after a null check on val; Swift needs a new binding (if let), with no smart-cast on stored properties.

Analogy: an Optional is a gift box that may be empty. if let opens it carefully; ! rips it open and explodes if nothing is inside.

Common interview traps.

  • Using ! "because I know it is not nil"; senior answer: use guard let with a meaningful failure.
  • Not knowing Optional is an enum with .some / .none.
  • Mixing up nil for a String? vs the empty string for text fields; model the difference deliberately.
  • Comparing Optional<Optional<Int>> accidentally via try? on old code (pre Swift 5 behaviour).

notes.title: Throwing functions, try, try? and try!
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin any function can throw, nothing in the signature says so (no checked exceptions), and callers use try/catch or runCatching. In Swift a function that can fail is marked throws, and every call site must be marked try. The error is passed back via a secondary return channel (no stack unwinding cost like C++ exceptions: it is an ordinary return with an error register).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum NetworkError: Error {
    case offline
    case badStatus(Int)
    case decoding(underlying: Error)
}

func fetchUser(id: Int) async throws -> User {
    let (data, response) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url(for: id))
    guard let http = response as? HTTPURLResponse else { throw NetworkError.offline }
    guard (200..<300).contains(http.statusCode) else { throw NetworkError.badStatus(http.statusCode) }
    do { return try JSONDecoder().decode(User.self, from: data) }
    catch { throw NetworkError.decoding(underlying: error) }
}
sealed class NetworkError : Exception() {
    object Offline : NetworkError()
    data class BadStatus(val code: Int) : NetworkError()
    data class Decoding(val underlying: Throwable) : NetworkError()
}

suspend fun fetchUser(id: Int): User {
    val resp = client.get(urlFor(id))
    if (!resp.isSuccessful) throw NetworkError.BadStatus(resp.code)
    try { return json.decodeFromString(resp.body) }
    catch (e: Exception) { throw NetworkError.Decoding(e) }
}

The four call forms:

Form Behaviour Kotlin analogue
try f() Propagates; enclosing function must throws or be in do/catch normal call
try? f() Returns T?; error discarded runCatching{}.getOrNull()
try! f() Traps on error (crash) !! on a failing result
do { try f() } catch { } Handle try/catch 
do {
    let user = try await fetchUser(id: 7)
    show(user)
} catch NetworkError.offline {
    showOfflineBanner()
} catch NetworkError.badStatus(let code) where code == 401 {
    signOut()
} catch let error as NetworkError {
    log(error)
} catch {
    // implicit `error` constant, type `any Error`
    log(error)
}

Facts to know:

  • catch clauses use the same pattern matching as switch. A do block without a catch-all requires an enclosing throwing context.
  • rethrows marks functions that throw only if their closure parameter throws (e.g. map).
  • defer runs on scope exit including on throw, like finally.
  • Error has no required methods. For user text conform to LocalizedError (errorDescription).
  • Cancellation: structured concurrency throws CancellationError (from Task.checkCancellation()) or URLError.cancelled; do not show these as user-visible failures.
  • Performance: Swift errors are cheap (existential box allocation for any Error, no unwinding tables), so throwing for ordinary control flow is acceptable, unlike in Java.
  • try! is accepted in tests and for compile-time-known inputs (e.g. a constant regex), nowhere else.

Real industry usage. JSONDecoder.decode throws DecodingError with cases .keyNotFound, .typeMismatch, .valueNotFound, .dataCorrupted; production apps log its codingPath into Sentry/Crashlytics. FileManager, Data(contentsOf:), SwiftData's modelContext.save() and Core Data try context.save() all throw. Alamofire's AFError is an enum wrapping underlying errors.

Analogy: throws is a fragile sticker on a parcel. Everyone who touches it must sign (try) to acknowledge, and someone downstream must have a plan for it breaking.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming try means the call is wrapped in a handler. It only marks the point of potential failure.
  • Using try? and losing the error; in production you almost never want to throw away the reason.
  • Catching error in a Task { } and forgetting that an unhandled throw inside an unstructured Task is silently stored in its Task.value.
  • Android mix-up: Kotlin CancellationException must be rethrown; the Swift equivalent is propagating CancellationError.

notes.title: Typed throws in Swift 6
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin has no typed errors for exceptions; people use Result<T, E> libraries (Arrow Either, kotlin-result) or sealed result classes for that. Swift 6 adds typed throws (SE-0413) to the language: throws(MyError).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum ValidationError: Error {
    case empty
    case tooShort(min: Int)
}

func validate(_ name: String) throws(ValidationError) {
    guard !name.isEmpty else { throw .empty }
    guard name.count >= 3 else { throw .tooShort(min: 3) }
}

do {
    try validate("ab")
} catch {
    // `error` is ValidationError here, not `any Error`
    switch error {
    case .empty: print("empty")
    case .tooShort(let min): print("need \(min)")
    }
}
sealed interface ValidationError {
    data object Empty : ValidationError
    data class TooShort(val min: Int) : ValidationError
}

fun validate(name: String): ValidationError? = when {
    name.isEmpty() -> ValidationError.Empty
    name.length < 3 -> ValidationError.TooShort(3)
    else -> null
}

Rules:

  • Plain throws is sugar for throws(any Error). A non-throwing function is sugar for throws(Never). That unification is why generic code such as map can propagate "whatever the closure throws" and become non-throwing when the closure is non-throwing.
  • Inside a do block, if all thrown errors are one concrete type the catch error has that type; otherwise it widens to any Error.
  • Typed throws removes the existential box: no heap allocation for the error, useful in embedded Swift and hot paths.
  • Type inference of closures' thrown type is limited in Swift 6.0; some code needs explicit throws(E) on the closure. Marked verify for exact inference rules in your Xcode version.
  • Apple guidance (from the SE-0413 text) is to prefer untyped throws for most application code, because error types leak into API and make evolution hard. Use typed throws for: a single closed set of errors inside a module, generic propagation, and low level / performance critical code.
  • Async: func f() async throws(MyError) is allowed. Task's failure type is the same idea (Task<Success, Failure: Error>), so Task<Int, Never> cannot throw. AsyncThrowingStream still uses any Error in the first release (verify for newer improvements).

Analogy: untyped throws is "something went wrong, open the mystery envelope". Typed throws is a form with a fixed list of tick boxes: the receiver knows the options in advance.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking throws(E) forces callers to catch exhaustively; do/catch with E still needs a catch-all only if other errors can escape.
  • Using typed throws across a public module boundary and then being unable to add a case without a breaking change (the same non-frozen enum problem).
  • Believing typed throws exists on Swift 5.x toolchains (it needs Swift 6.0 compiler; runtime back-deploys because it is mostly a compile-time feature, but verify).

notes.title: The Result type and when to use it
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin has kotlin.Result<T> (success or Throwable) and runCatching; many projects add sealed class Resource<T>. Swift has Result<Success, Failure: Error>, in the standard library since Swift 5.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func parse(_ text: String) -> Result<Int, ParseError> {
    guard let n = Int(text) else { return .failure(.notANumber(text)) }
    return .success(n)
}

switch parse("42") {
case .success(let n): print(n)
case .failure(let e): print(e)
}

let doubled = parse("21").map { $0 * 2 }                 // Result<Int, ParseError>
let value = try parse("21").get()                        // converts back into throws
let wrapped = Result { try JSONDecoder().decode(User.self, from: data) } // Result<User, any Error>
fun parse(text: String): Result<Int> =
    text.toIntOrNull()?.let { Result.success(it) }
        ?: Result.failure(ParseError.NotANumber(text))

parse("42").fold(onSuccess = { println(it) }, onFailure = { println(it) })
val doubled = parse("21").map { it * 2 }
val value = parse("21").getOrThrow()
val wrapped = runCatching { json.decodeFromString<User>(text) }

When to use Result today:

Situation Preferred
async function that can fail async throws
Completion handler API you cannot change Result in the callback
Storing an outcome as a value (cache, state, Combine, TCA action) Result
Collecting many outcomes (batch import) [Result<T, E>]
Synchronous function throws

Swift's own Result was introduced to tidy completion-handler code: (Result<Data, Error>) -> Void. You will meet this in old codebases (pre-iOS 15) and in libraries such as Alamofire (response.result), Moya and Firebase wrappers. Modern code uses async throws and keeps Result only where an outcome must be stored or transmitted as a value.

Bridging callbacks with Result:

func load() async throws -> Data {
    try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { cont in
        legacyLoad { (result: Result<Data, Error>) in
            cont.resume(with: result)       // Result is accepted directly
        }
    }
}

Other points: Result has map, flatMap, mapError, flatMapError. Failure must conform to Error; use Never for results that cannot fail. With typed throws, Result<T, MyError> and throws(MyError) are now two views of the same thing.

Real industry usage. TCA actions like case response(Result<[Todo], Error>); Combine's .catch / Future use Result in the promise callback; SwiftUI fileImporter(onCompletion:) returns Result<URL, Error>.

Analogy: Result is a sealed envelope marked either "delivered" or "returned to sender": you can store it, pass it around, and open it later, unlike a thrown error that must be handled right now.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Result for every async function (a Kotlin/RxJava habit); in Swift async code throws is idiomatic.
  • Using Result<T, Error> where Error makes the failure type uselessly broad.
  • Forgetting that try? on a Result.get() throws away the error again.

notes.title: Never and Never-returning functions
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Kotlin's Nothing is the bottom type for throw and TODO(). Swift's equivalent is Never, defined as an enum with no cases, so a value of that type can never exist.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func crash(_ message: String) -> Never {
    fatalError(message)           // Swift standard library: returns Never
}

func parseOrDie(_ s: String) -> Int {
    guard let n = Int(s) else { crash("bad input") }   // compiler knows control stops
    return n
}

// Never as a generic argument: "this can never fail / never emit"
let always: Result<Int, Never> = .success(1)
let value = always.get()                       // no `try` needed for Failure == Never
let publisher = Just(1)                        // Combine: Just<Output>.Failure == Never
fun crash(message: String): Nothing = error(message)

fun parseOrDie(s: String): Int =
    s.toIntOrNull() ?: crash("bad input")

val always: Result<Int> = Result.success(1)

Where Never appears:

  • fatalError, preconditionFailure, exit, and abort return Never. assertionFailure does not (it is a no-op in release).
  • Task<Int, Never>: a task that cannot throw. Task { ... } with a non-throwing body gets Failure == Never.
  • AsyncStream<Element> has Failure == Never; AsyncThrowingStream has Error.
  • SwiftUI.View.body of primitive views is Never (e.g. Text.body: Never). Core views terminate the body recursion with Never.
  • Since SE-0396, Never conforms to Equatable, Hashable, Comparable, Codable (verify the exact conformance list in your toolchain).

Production note: fatalError shows up in crash logs as EXC_BREAKPOINT / SIGTRAP with the message in the crash reporter's "Application Specific Information". Use it only for programmer errors, never for user or network states.

Analogy: Never is the door painted on a wall: you can write it into the blueprint (the type system), but no one will ever walk through.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing Void ((), one value) with Never (zero values).
  • Putting fatalError in code paths reachable by bad server data; use a thrown error.
  • Not knowing that Result<T, Never> removes the need for try.

notes.title: Designing an error taxonomy for an app
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. On Android you might have a sealed class AppError mapped from IOException, HttpException and SQLiteException in a repository, and a UiText shown by a ViewModel. The iOS shape is the same: lower layers throw specific errors, the domain maps them, and the presentation layer turns them into user messages and actions.

UI (SwiftUI view)          shows message, retry button, sign-in screen
        ^
ViewModel (@Observable)    maps AppError -> UiState.failed(AlertContent)
        ^
Repository / UseCase       maps DataError -> AppError (domain)
        ^
Data layer                 URLError, DecodingError, SwiftData errors -> DataError
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Data layer: precise, internal
enum DataError: Error {
    case transport(URLError)
    case http(status: Int, body: Data?)
    case decoding(DecodingError)
    case storage(any Error)
}

// Domain layer: what the product cares about
enum AppError: Error, Equatable {
    case offline
    case unauthorized
    case notFound
    case rateLimited(retryAfter: TimeInterval?)
    case server
    case unknown
}

extension AppError {
    init(_ error: DataError) {
        switch error {
        case .transport(let e) where e.code == .notConnectedToInternet: self = .offline
        case .http(401, _): self = .unauthorized
        case .http(404, _): self = .notFound
        case .http(429, _): self = .rateLimited(retryAfter: nil)
        case .http(let s, _) where s >= 500: self = .server
        default: self = .unknown
        }
    }

    var userMessage: String {
        switch self {
        case .offline: String(localized: "You're offline.")
        case .unauthorized: String(localized: "Please sign in again.")
        case .notFound: String(localized: "We couldn't find that.")
        case .rateLimited: String(localized: "Too many requests. Try again shortly.")
        case .server, .unknown: String(localized: "Something went wrong.")
        }
    }

    var isRetryable: Bool {
        switch self {
        case .offline, .rateLimited, .server: true
        default: false
        }
    }
}
sealed interface AppError {
    data object Offline : AppError
    data object Unauthorized : AppError
    data object NotFound : AppError
    data class RateLimited(val retryAfterSec: Long?) : AppError
    data object Server : AppError
    data object Unknown : AppError
}

fun Throwable.toAppError(): AppError = when (this) {
    is UnknownHostException -> AppError.Offline
    is HttpException -> when (code()) {
        401 -> AppError.Unauthorized
        404 -> AppError.NotFound
        429 -> AppError.RateLimited(null)
        in 500..599 -> AppError.Server
        else -> AppError.Unknown
    }
    else -> AppError.Unknown
}

Design rules:

  1. Separate three audiences: the developer (log everything, with underlying error), the user (short localized text, an action) and the program (retry? sign out? ignore?). One enum with computed properties like isRetryable keeps the three in sync.
  2. Do not leak implementation types upward (e.g. SQLiteError in a View). Map at layer boundaries, and keep the original in an underlying payload for logs.
  3. Cancellation is not an error to show. Filter CancellationError and URLError.cancelled in one place.
  4. Programmer errors crash (precondition, fatalError); environment errors throw.
  5. Make enums Equatable so you can test them with #expect(error == .offline).
  6. Public frameworks: mark enums @frozen only if they will truly never change; otherwise clients must use @unknown default.
  7. Localisation: use LocalizedError (errorDescription, failureReason, recoverySuggestion) when the error will be displayed by system UI such as .alert(isPresented:error:).
struct AppErrorAlert: LocalizedError {
    let base: AppError
    var errorDescription: String? { base.userMessage }
}

Testing with Swift Testing:

import Testing

@Test func mapsOffline() {
    let e = AppError(.transport(URLError(.notConnectedToInternet)))
    #expect(e == .offline)
    #expect(e.isRetryable)
}

@Test func validationThrows() {
    #expect(throws: ValidationError.empty) { try validate("") }
}

Production incident patterns:

  • Generic "Something went wrong" everywhere: support cannot triage. Fix: log DataError with status code and request id, show the generic text.
  • Retry loop on 401: the client retries the refresh forever and gets rate limited. Fix: map to .unauthorized once, sign out, stop.
  • try? in a persistence layer: save failures silently lose data; users report "my notes vanished". Fix: surface .storage to monitoring (Sentry, Crashlytics non-fatal, MetricKit diagnostics).
  • try! on decoding server JSON: one new field type crashes all users on launch (EXC_BREAKPOINT). Fix: decode defensively and map DecodingError.

Real industry practice: Apple's own frameworks use domain-specific error types (URLError, CocoaError, DecodingError, CLError, LAError), Alamofire wraps everything in AFError, Firebase uses NSError codes (legacy bridging: error as NSError and .domain/.code). Airbnb and Uber architecture talks describe mapping transport errors to domain errors in repositories, as above.

Analogy: the taxonomy is a hospital triage desk. Paramedics (data layer) report exact injuries; triage (domain) assigns urgency and next steps; the patient (user) only hears "wait here, we'll call you".

Common interview traps.

  • Using one giant enum Error across the whole app, which makes every switch huge and every layer coupled.
  • Showing error.localizedDescription of a raw URLError to users (the text is technical and localised by the system).
  • Android vs iOS: expecting a global uncaught exception handler to show a dialog; iOS has no equivalent, an uncaught Swift runtime trap kills the process immediately (only NSException has an uncaught handler).
  • Forgetting Sendable: errors thrown across actor or task boundaries must be Sendable in Swift 6; enums with only Sendable payloads get it automatically, but any Error already requires Sendable.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Swift enums are value-type algebraic data types: a single enum covers what Kotlin does with sealed classes, Optional and Result.
  • switch is always exhaustive; use pattern matching (case let, where, ranges, tuples) and @unknown default for Apple enums.
  • indirect boxes recursive cases on the heap; deep recursion still overflows the stack.
  • Optional is enum { none, some }; avoid !, prefer guard let and ??.
  • Errors: throws + try at every call site, try? loses the reason, try! crashes.
  • Swift 6 typed throws (throws(E)) removes the existential and makes catch typed; use it for closed, internal error sets, keep untyped throws in public app APIs.
  • Result still matters for stored outcomes and callback bridging; async throws is the default for new code.
  • Never is the empty enum: fatalError returns it, Result<T, Never> cannot fail.
  • Build an error taxonomy by layer: data errors, domain AppError, user message and retry policy; always filter cancellation; crash only for programmer bugs.
  • Unverified: exact closure inference rules for typed throws and Never conformance list in the newest toolchains (verify).
